subtopic: ASSISTANCE FOR AGRICULTURAL SETTLEMENT AND REHABILITATION AND DEVELOPMENT OF NATURAL AND OTHER RESOURCES
speechtext:
This particular subsection is nothing less than coercion as far as the unemployed are concerned, and I am surprised that the Minister of Labour would bring forward such a proposition. As you know, Mr. Chairman, many of the people on relief in the larger cities are skilled workers, bricklayers, carpenters, and so on. I am surprised at the minister, if he is a real labour man, proposing such a coercive bill as the one now before us. This business of relief was all right during the darker days of the depression, but now the first of May is only about ten days away, and many of these people who are in receipt of relief were hoping to get back to work at union or prevailing rates, in construction work and in other lines, on the first of next month. I doubt whether this bill is legal, as a matter of fact, because it refers to the "general interest of Canada" and there is no such legal phrase. We may be sure that the house of philology, the other chamber, will change that to "the general advantage of Canada."
On behalf of the industrial workers of the country I wish to object to the principle of this and every other subsection of this clause. If the government of the day would study the problem a little more, as it has been studied in other countries, they would not go about it in this way. I have here the report of the Senate of the United States of 1927 on unemployment. Senator Couzens was chairman, and I believe this bill was largely copied from the United States bill having to do with the same question. In that country they grant money to the larger municipalities. Why should this question continue to be made a political football in the various provinces? Some of the provinces are bankrupt; one has announced that it wants to get rid of relief altogether and turn it back to the dominion. Where are the funds for this bill to come from? They will come from the earnings of the industrial workers of Ontario and Quebec very largely, and my proposition is this: These agreements wdth regard to relief should be made directly with the larger municipalities. Why deal with a third party when that third party does not handle relief at all but merely passes on the money? Here we have A, B and C, A the dominion, B the province and C the municipality, and B should be eliminated and wTe should deal direct

Unemployment
with the municipalities. If the federal government is conscientious and consistent about this matter of the municipalities and the provinces why do they not turn over the relief funds in the larger centres of population directly to the municipalities? In the larger centres like Toronto and Hamilton they run these things free from politics. This is giving labour the greatest black eye it will ever get. This is a coercion bill. The government has no right to coerce a citizen who has never been on relief before and compel him if he works to take relief rates not union rates. I and the other Toronto members represent an industrial riding in which sixty-five per cent of the people own their own homes. Many of these men never knew what it was to be on relief until this depression came with its disturbance of the industrial equilibrium, but they have been forced on relief, and the loan sharks have got hold of some of them. Are we going to allow the relief officer who handles this fund to say to a worker, "You will either take this job at the wages offered or go off relief altogether," Thus forcing him to take a mere pittance? The province should never come into this matter. This clause means that the railways have been made the favourites of this parliament; they are to be handed a large sum for equipment. Why should the railways get a hand-out like that, and the municipalities not get a cent? If these are to be public works, proper consideration should be given to the question of how these relief rates are going to interfere permanently with the wage scales of the skilled workers who have been driven to take relief through no fault of their own.
I would like to help the government on this employment question, but there has been so much red tape about the whole thing; it is largely a conglomeration of words; the metaphysical language of the minister in almost every address has beclouded the whole question. With the first of May only ten days away I do not know what is going to become of the unemployed in Toronto and Hamilton and other cites of Ontario. Toronto is a solvent municipality; it can pay one hundred cents on the dollar and can borrow money at the lowest rate in the dominion. It is not only looking after its own relief but is contributing $83,000,000 to the federal treasury this year. I say on behalf of the workers there that this is not a fair deal to industrial workers who have never been on relief before. It is very unfair to leave this in the hands of the provinces and the large corporations without any protection to the workers. What is the labour department for? As I understand it
the labour department should be up and doing to protect the worker.
I protest against the principle involved in this bill. It is against the liberty of the subject. It is a coercion bill; it is going to force the skilled workers who should earn seven or eight dollars a day to take $1.35 or whatever the province may say, and some of the provinces are bankrupt and cannot pay their way.

subtopic: ASSISTANCE FOR AGRICULTURAL SETTLEMENT AND REHABILITATION AND DEVELOPMENT OF NATURAL AND OTHER RESOURCES
speechtext: Why is there no provision here to permit the governor in council to deal with municipalities, or are they included?

subtopic: ASSISTANCE FOR AGRICULTURAL SETTLEMENT AND REHABILITATION AND DEVELOPMENT OF NATURAL AND OTHER RESOURCES
speechtext: In the past, without exception, I think, the dominion government have dealt with the municipalities through the provinces.

subtopic: ASSISTANCE FOR AGRICULTURAL SETTLEMENT AND REHABILITATION AND DEVELOPMENT OF NATURAL AND OTHER RESOURCES
speechtext:
Where municipalities are bankrupt, as some of them are, it is taking an extraordinary position to lend to private corporations such as the railways, and yet take no power to assist the municipalities where large numbers of unemployed are now concentrated. It also misses an opportunity to work out a practical scheme of cooperation between the dominion, the provincial and the municipal governments, whereby as supplementary to public works there could be incorporated plans of social service as permanent measures for eliminating certain types of extremely persistent and difficult unemployment. At the mayors' conference the men who probably are closer to the unemployment relief problem than any others thought it would be advisable to have a much greater measure of cooperation than has . existed in the past between the three political executives that now govern the people of Canada. Speaking from a practical point of view and from some practical experience, I believe that one cause of failure in both the British and the American recovery programs is the fact that they refused to recognize the municipal governments as channels through which measures of unemployment relief could be established on a permanent basis. The situation in Vancouver is not a bit different from what it is in any other city in the dominion. In Ottawa, Montreal, Quebec, Windsor or Winnipeg you find an ever increasing accumulation of persistent unemployment that cannot be relieved by work on railways or by what are commonly called public works. We are not at the end of the depression, although this is the seventh year of it, and to leave out the municipalities and carry on as we have in the past, dealing through the provinces and refusing to recognize the muni-
Unemployment

cipal governments as having an immediate relation with the dominion government, is a serious and fundamental barrier to success in the unemployment relief program.
I do not know how far the government feel that the municipalities can carry the burden of the unemployable. There are two phases of that particular branch of the problem which must be considered. The first is that the municipalities, as such are not able to meet the ordinary needs of the people. The social service problems which have been developed as a part of the functions of municipal government are far beyond the revenue powers of municipal administration. But more than that, out of the existing depression a large number of people have developed into unemployable public charges, and this condition has brought the totals up to far greater numbers than were ever contemplated when the assumption was established that, through levies on its own taxpayers, the municipal government should maintain those in destitution who were resident within a city. I know that the problem of health service in many cities has been carried on only because in a spirit of charity medical doctors have given professional services for which they have not been paid. If there is to be no cooperation between the dominion government and municipal governments throughout the dominion, then it does seem to me that municipal governments are facing a very serious position, and one which they should not have to continue to face. I do not suppose it is the intention of the government to throw into a condition of destitution and starvation those who are now dependent upon municipalities, and if through the municipalities and out of. the limited funds to be made available by parliament some arrangement is not made now for the care of these people it will practically mean receiverships for municipalities from one end of Canada to the other. The real problem comes down to this: When men in municipal governments are faced with the choice of paying interest on their bonds and meeting their debt charges, or appropriating their available funds to taking care of the destitute in their respective areas, they are going to choose on the side of humanity. That means default; it means receiverships, and, has already meant receiverships in two hundred and fifty-three municipalities across the dominion. The situation is not one to be blinked at; it is not one the responsibility for which-may be ignored, and it does not seem to me that the bill anticipates the action which must be taken on this problem before the year is out.

subtopic: ASSISTANCE FOR AGRICULTURAL SETTLEMENT AND REHABILITATION AND DEVELOPMENT OF NATURAL AND OTHER RESOURCES
speechtext:
I believe every municipality in Canada appreciates what the government did in that regard, and the admonition to the provinces to pass on the benefits of the increased grant, but notwithstanding that admonition, some of the provinces did not pass it on. I do not think any of them passed on the full amount. I know that while in British Columbia the province was fairly generous with the municipalities, at the same time it pointed out that as a provincial government their load was far more than they could carry. Of course the natural tendency of the provincial government is to balance its budget and let municipal governments take care of themselves. Already we have two hundred and fifty-three municipalities in default, and we are now threatened with a situation in Montreal, Windsor, Calgary, Moose Jaw, Victoria and other cities which is going to spread. Whether under the constitution or under the practice which has grown out of it, the fact remains that each municipal government is a definite part of the political executive of the dominion. The municipalities are administering the affairs of more than half the total population of the dominion and have under their jurisdiction an enormous portion of the total accumulated wealth of the Canadian people. That whole structure is in jeopardy.
But more than that, and quite apart from the financial angle, does the government think that in connection with the problems of education, the advancement of health measures, the development of effective superannuation allowances, mothers' pensions and a great many other social services, which are now part and parcel of our administrative

Unemployment
activity, there is no opportunity for the federal government to associate with municipal governments in opening up a permanent channel through which destitution can be alleviated and employment developed. Because that, I take it, is to be one of the plans of permanent employment relief to be developed. If the dominion government cannot enter into arrangements with the municipal governments, how can that be worked out?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: ASSISTANCE FOR AGRICULTURAL SETTLEMENT AND REHABILITATION AND DEVELOPMENT OF NATURAL AND OTHER RESOURCES
speechtext: May I answer my hon. friend at once by directing his attention to what has been done by the Dominion government in connection with old age pensions. In this one particular, not to mention others, the federal government has granted large sums for an all important social service carried on in the provinces and w'hich immediately benefits the municipalities, but has had to do so having regard to restrictions as to procedure imposed upon it. Where the federal government has made grants in aid in connection with old age pensions the grants have been to the provinces. It is only by that method, subject to such supervision as the dominion and provincial governments working together may have arranged, that dominion funds have been distributed to the municipalities.

subtopic: ASSISTANCE FOR AGRICULTURAL SETTLEMENT AND REHABILITATION AND DEVELOPMENT OF NATURAL AND OTHER RESOURCES
speechtext:
I should like to have a
minute, so that the minister may make clear beyond peradventure what is meant by subsection 1 of section 3. We have heard many members of the government state that it is proposed that parliament shall be asked to appropriate sums of money for specific purposes. This section indicates, however, that -not for specific purposes at all, but out of a lump sum-appropriations may be made by the governor in council, and not by parliament. So that this much talked of parliamentary control vanishes; all we have left is that parliament votes one or ten millions as the case may be, and out of that, moneys are paid under agreements made by the governor in council, which is the practice that was so much condemned in the past. The only parliamentary control is with respect to the voting of the sum of money out of which these various works are to be undertaken.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: ASSISTANCE FOR AGRICULTURAL SETTLEMENT AND REHABILITATION AND DEVELOPMENT OF NATURAL AND OTHER RESOURCES
speechtext: That is the effective control. When parliament appropriates public moneys it knows what it is doing, but when the governor in council takes money out of the public treasury without any previous appropriation by parliament, parliament does not know what the government is doing. The result is as we now know to our cost-, that millions of dollars have had to be accounted for when there is no longer possibility of any control, at the end of the year with respect to which parliament had no previous knowledge whatever. I think my right hon. friend laboured this point at great length just before the recess and was effectively answered at that time; moreover, the subsection passed before the recess. My right hon. friend sometimes accuses me of having an obsession, but I think this is becoming an obsession with him.

subtopic: ASSISTANCE FOR AGRICULTURAL SETTLEMENT AND REHABILITATION AND DEVELOPMENT OF NATURAL AND OTHER RESOURCES
speechtext: It is no obsession. I am simply pointing out that there is no appropriation by this parliament of moneys for specific undertakings.

speechtext:
My other question was
with respect to the demand for farm labour. There is some demand for farm labour in some parts of the prairie provinces, particularly in southern Saskatchewan, but the men are being offered between eight and ten dollars a month. It simply means that the average young man would not have sufficient money to pay for the shoes and gloves he would wear out. This does not offer any counterattraction to the amount of money paid in the camps, nor is it a counter-attraction to railway construction work that may turn up in the future. It is not the fault of the agricultural population, for they cannot afford 12739-125
to pay more. Does the Department of Labour propose any scheme by which it may subsidize the farmer in order to help him to hire labour? If it is proposed to subsidize railways or corporations and to cooperate with them to enable them to hire extra help, is there any method whereby the agricultural population can be similarly assisted?

subtopic: ASSISTANCE FOR AGRICULTURAL SETTLEMENT AND REHABILITATION AND DEVELOPMENT OF NATURAL AND OTHER RESOURCES
speechtext:
That is a proposal which
has received some consideration in the past and will no doubt deserve consideration in the future. In the early experience of the farm placement scheme the dominion government contributed $5 a month which was paid to the man and the provincial government contributed $5 which was paid to the farmer. Subsequently that was abandoned and, in the last two years certainly, the dominion government has paid $5 to the man and the farmer has been content to receive that man's assistance in return for board and lodging. That applied only during the winter months in connection with the farm placement scheme. There is not under immediate consideration any plan by which the dominion government or, I assume, the provincial governments, will subsidize farmers for the employment of farm labour at this season of the year. I admit it is a direction which may profitably be explored.

subtopic: ASSISTANCE FOR AGRICULTURAL SETTLEMENT AND REHABILITATION AND DEVELOPMENT OF NATURAL AND OTHER RESOURCES
speechtext:
The minister said that
farmers were satisfied to receive the services of the man. That is true but only to a limited extent. I know for a fact that many farmers would be mighty glad to have a man on their farms in the winter months repairing buildings, harness and machinery and fattening some extra cattle, but they cannot afford to pay him; rather, they cannot afford to board him. Some time ago in this house I advanced a scheme to pay the man $10 a month to work on the farm and to subsidize the farmer to the same extent, and then it would be allowing only $20 a month to maintain the man on the farm. It is a fact, and hon. members know it, that under the present scheme it costs the taxpayers over $50 a month to keep these single unemployed men in the relief camps. I suggest to the government that our unemployment problem is not likely to be solved by next winter and we shall have to follow the same course we are following now and keep these men on the land. The government should consider very seriously the policy of bonusing the farmers for keeping these men on the farms, because I believe that by that policy the relief camps could be emptied. It is worthy of consideration and I believe the minister is considering that very proposal in a favourable light.

subtopic: ASSISTANCE FOR AGRICULTURAL SETTLEMENT AND REHABILITATION AND DEVELOPMENT OF NATURAL AND OTHER RESOURCES
speechtext: I wish to bring to the attention of the minister in this connection certain facts of which I have become aware. At Transcona, where the Canadian National has its shops, there occurred recently a layoff of about 300 men. These men had been occupied largely in the building of refrigerator cars through an appropriation made last year of $15,000,000, which was to be expended in the railway shops throughout the country, and I assume that the reason these men are being laid off now is that this appropriation has been expended. During the Easter recess I attended a meeting at Transcona, where there is prevalent among the men the feeling that the laying off of these regular men at the present time is not a very seeming attitude on the part of the government. These regular employees were getting as a matter of fact only eighteen days a month, and the feeling is that they should not be laid off while money is being spent to put to work single men who have been in the camps. Every man should have his turn; there is no doubt about that. But in laying off a regular employee who has a family you lay off several individuals and put them on relief, whereas in the relief camps only single individuals without dependents are involved. I was not able to give an explanation and was on the verge of wiring the minister but I decided to wait until I got to Ottawa and could see him personally. Now that the matter is before the house it is perhaps not amiss to bring up this question.

subtopic: ASSISTANCE FOR AGRICULTURAL SETTLEMENT AND REHABILITATION AND DEVELOPMENT OF NATURAL AND OTHER RESOURCES
speechtext:
According to the present wording of subsection 2 there will be shut out from employment on relief works in Ontario a good many young men who are not on relief. I have received a letter from a commercial traveller who has been through New Ontario, having visited seven or eight of the leading centres where relief works are being carried out, and he complains that the men who are engaged on relief works are mainly from the continent of Europe and it is impossible for young Canadians to get jobs there. The young Canadian leaves the large city and goes to that part of the country and there he finds that under the provincial regulations he is not qualified for relief work because he is not on relief. The other day at Kirkland Lake eight young Canadians were locked up as vagrants-young fellows born in Ontario- their only crime being that they could not get work. It is all very well for the minister to put in this bill all this language about the employment of persons available and competent. Those men who come from Europe are always available in New Ontario not only for government road works but in the mines. People of this class are catered to because they take lower wages and if they are injured they say nothing about it. The summer is coming and young Canadians are looking for work. Many of their fathers are on relief; they do not like to hang around the house when there is not enough food to go round, and the result is that they "ride the rods" on our heavily subsidized railway. Then they are haled before the magistrate and, without having a chance to defend themselves, without a lawyer, they are landed in some gaol in New Ontario. I think the minister should make it possible for these young men to get work, but according to the present wording of this provision this class of young Canadians will be shut out, as they are not now on relief. If they apply for work in northern Ontario they are promptly locked up. Where is the magna charta? The trouble is there are too many catch phrases in this bill and not enough common sense. No practical way has been provided of getting people off relief and the dole as is being done in many other countries. I have studied this situation for many years and in 1927 I tried to get the government of the day to do the very thing they are proposing to do to-day.
Summer is coming on and many of these young people will be leaving high school. I am referring largely to the high school population. These young men do not want to keep on studying; they want to go up north and do something to develop new Ontario, but when they go there they are

Unemployment
locked up and given eight days by some magistrate on a charge of vagrancy. That particular section of the vagrancy law with reference to not having visible means of support or who himself lives without employment, should be stricken out. These young men were trying to get a job on relief work being carried out by the provincial government with the assistance of the dominion government. In the case of federal works in cities the requirement is that there shall be a year's residence, but some of these people who have been given jobs have not been in the country that long. They are able to beat the regulations and get work when our own Canadians cannot get it. Some restriction should be imposed on the granting of relief to the provinces to the end that young people leaving school who want to work shall not be discriminated against because of the language used in this section.

subtopic: ASSISTANCE FOR AGRICULTURAL SETTLEMENT AND REHABILITATION AND DEVELOPMENT OF NATURAL AND OTHER RESOURCES
speechtext: I do not want to lay unnecessary emphasis upon the farm labour question, but I do want to urge upon the minister the need of immediate action. Thousands of farmers on the prairies will be going on the land in the course of the next few weeks. They will not be needing help next winter; they will be needing it now, this summer and this fall. Some scheme should be evolved under which these men could be placed on the land and their wages supplemented by the government. This would be good policy from the standpoint of the morale of the men and the farmers, and it would also save considerable money. Some time ago I quoted from a sessional paper to show that the average cost of keeping men in the relief camps was $50.70 per man per month. This shows that these camps have not been a financial success. Because of the heavy overhead the cost per month per man varied all the way from $18.20 to $233.30. I know there were conditions present to explain that high figure, but the average figure of S50.70 is too high. Many of these men could be placed on farms so that they could take their normal places in the community. I urge upon the minister that he consider this point very seriously.

subtopic: ASSISTANCE FOR AGRICULTURAL SETTLEMENT AND REHABILITATION AND DEVELOPMENT OF NATURAL AND OTHER RESOURCES
speechtext: Shall the subsection carry?

subtopic: ASSISTANCE FOR AGRICULTURAL SETTLEMENT AND REHABILITATION AND DEVELOPMENT OF NATURAL AND OTHER RESOURCES
speechtext: I want an answer to my question.

subtopic: ASSISTANCE FOR AGRICULTURAL SETTLEMENT AND REHABILITATION AND DEVELOPMENT OF NATURAL AND OTHER RESOURCES
speechtext: I understand my hon. friend was inquiring as to agreements made by the dominion government for relief purposes?

subtopic: ASSISTANCE FOR AGRICULTURAL SETTLEMENT AND REHABILITATION AND DEVELOPMENT OF NATURAL AND OTHER RESOURCES
speechtext: We have heard about the railway agreement; I should like to know what other agreements are in contemplation.

subtopic: ASSISTANCE FOR AGRICULTURAL SETTLEMENT AND REHABILITATION AND DEVELOPMENT OF NATURAL AND OTHER RESOURCES
speechtext: The normal agreements will be those with the provinces. That has always been the case in the past. There is a contingent provision in a later section for agreements with corporations, partnerships or individuals. I have no hesitation in saying that under this bill the normal type of agreement in the future, as in the past, will be agreements with the provinces.

subtopic: ASSISTANCE FOR AGRICULTURAL SETTLEMENT AND REHABILITATION AND DEVELOPMENT OF NATURAL AND OTHER RESOURCES
speechtext:
From time to time as
emergencies arose the provinces made application to the dominion government and presented proposals. I have in mind one with reference to the city of Winnipeg covering the construction of an auditorium and a sewage system involving some $4,000,000. The government considered that proposal and then joined with the provincial government in carrying it out. That was done from time to time. Under this peculiarly worded section, unless all these agreements are consummated before parliament rises, no such agreement could be made to meet an emergency which might arise next winter. There seems to me to be unwarranted optimism on the part of the government that there will be no emergency arising next year; I think there will be more need for emergency activities next year than there was last year. Subsection 2 of section 4 is an omnibus provision which covers the whole section. It covers not only agreements made with corporations and partnerships but also those made with the provinces. Under this subsection no agreement made between a province and the dominion shall be binding upon the dominion until approved by resolution of the House of Commons. If financial assistance is needed for a provincial or municipal enterprise, there is no question that it would come under this section 4, and if the government wished to place all responsibility on the provincial and municipal authorities it could say that parliament had tied its hands, that it could not do anything until parliament convened again. The government could say that a resolution of parliament would be necessary before it could spend dominion government money on a program of relief.

subtopic: ASSISTANCE FOR AGRICULTURAL SETTLEMENT AND REHABILITATION AND DEVELOPMENT OF NATURAL AND OTHER RESOURCES
speechtext: Under an agreement.

subtopic: ASSISTANCE FOR AGRICULTURAL SETTLEMENT AND REHABILITATION AND DEVELOPMENT OF NATURAL AND OTHER RESOURCES
speechtext:
If that is the alternative,
then the dominion government must be prepared to assume the whole responsibility should the provincial and municipal authorities find themselves unable to take care of
Unemployment

the unemployment situation. Surely there is no necessity of tying down to a resolution of parliament the power of the dominion government to meet an emergency. Surely we must have learned something from what has taken place in the Argentine, in Australia, in Great Britain and in the United States as to how this problem can be worked out. The problem is far from solved in Great Britain to-day, and they are proceeding along exploratory channels. If parliament passes this section, the government of the day will be placed in the position of being able to say that it cannot do anything because parliament has tied its hands. The government can say that it is placed in the position of being unable to assume a general load because parliament has not voted enough money. This section 4 will place the government in a condition of impotency if the amount appropriated is a small one and is arrived at on the assumption that the provinces and cities can carry this load. Speaking as one who knows of the limitations of municipal financing in Canada, I can tell you that they cannot continue to carry the load they have been carrying in the past. In the United States, in Great Britain and in Australia that has been recognized, and national governments are moving to assume larger proportions of the burden. It may be, of course, that they are all wrong; it may be that in some miraculous way we in Canada are going to escape this horrible and appalling scourge of unemployment, and of course if that happens it does not matter what is in the bill, but I do not think there is any reason for any such conclusion. On the contrary, on every hand evidence indicates that the problem of unemployment is definitely intensifying and becoming more persistent and more emergent. With all due respect to the desire of the government to have parliament in control I am afraid that this section is going to reduce the power of the government to function.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: ASSISTANCE FOR AGRICULTURAL SETTLEMENT AND REHABILITATION AND DEVELOPMENT OF NATURAL AND OTHER RESOURCES
speechtext: May I ask my hon. friend if it is his idea that the unemployment problem is going to be solved by removing the control of parliament? Is that what he is advocating?

subtopic: ASSISTANCE FOR AGRICULTURAL SETTLEMENT AND REHABILITATION AND DEVELOPMENT OF NATURAL AND OTHER RESOURCES
speechtext:
No, but I do say that
parliament should be able to impose responsibilities on the government and should be able to give the government power to carry out aid fulfil those responsibilities. I quite agree that probably it would not be wise to give the government blank cheque spending power, bi t I do not think the dominion government is following the precedent established by other
1 Mr. McGeer.3
governments, either in Great Britain or the United States, in tying down to such detail work parliament's obligation to resolve on each specific agreement. How in the world is this parliament going to settle down, for instance, and discuss every resolution that might be necessary in order to consummate agreements to be entered into with an organization such as the Reconstruction Finance Corporation in the United States, for instance? How in the world does this government contemplate entering into agreements with corporations, partnerships and individuals that are going to improve the unemployment situation? That is properly the work of an organization such as the Reconstruction Finance Corporation in the United States. Is this parliament going to discuss and resolve upon details of administration of that kind? It must do so if it complies with this section. From time to time our problems of unemployment relief, as I have said, may be relieved or become intensified, but this section contemplates that the whole program of unemployment relief that is to be prosecuted, so far as it depends upon agreements or arrangements with private enterprise or with provincial and municipal governments, must be resolved upon and consummated before this parliament rises; otherwise there is no provision for carrying on.
I think that would be a very happy situation if the government were prepared to say, "Here is our plan of unemployment relief. We propose to do this and that, and to do it in this certain way." But parliament is asked to blindly tie the hands of the government without having the least intimation of the actual administrative program of unemployment relief. All we have heard so far is a vague indication that the government cannot spend money except under certain very specific limitations, and we have heard also that in some way, by arrangement with the railways, some ten thousand men are to be given work at twenty-five cents an hour. Well, is that the government's unemployment program? Personally I am sure it is not; I think there must be many other things in contemplation which may become the subject of agreements. Then is it neoessary to have each of these agreements resolved upon by parliament? I hardly think there is any justification for any such restriction. Surely if parliament gives the government broad power to carry on public works, to act in cooperation with the railways or with the provincial governments or in other ways in order to work out this unemployment problem, we need not sit here considering the details of every contract to be entered into.

speechtext:
I returned from the west this morning and in my part of the country, as far as I can find out, nothing has been done to provide farm help. We know from experience, and since the opening of the session evidence has been produced here, that farm help cannot get from the relief centres to the farms without some assistance, and we also know that when they do get on the farms they are not paid enough to encourage them to make any definite attempt to secure this work. I believe they are being paid more in the camps than they are offered for farm work. Some men of whom I have knowledge are working for $5 to $10 a month, and I think in fairness to the farmers and to the farm workers something definite should be done right away.
As far as the farmers are concerned I do not see how they are going to pay any higher wages than they have been paying, when you consider what they have been receiving for their products during the past six years. A few weeks ago a bill was passed under which I believe the farmers have been chiselled, if
1	might use that word, out of some of the money they should have had. I am referring now to the 1930 equalization bill.

That is all very fine, Mr. Chairman, but I want to point out that the farmers cannot put in their crops without hired help. Hired help cannot walk from the relief centres to the jobs, and I think it is up to this parliament to get busy and do something that will
get the help to these jobs. The farmers are expected to pay their debts, but without help they cannot put in their crops, and I think it is up to this government to do something for those people.

I had been waiting until we came to section 4 before offering one or two observations, but the discussion has opened up in such a manner that I think it necessary to say something at this stage.
Before the Easter recess we passed Bill No. 14, by which parliament authorized the setting up of a council; and I think I am interpreting the policy of the government correctly when I say that the object of setting up that council was to relieve the government of much detail and to secure the cooperation of experienced persons in entering into agreements and so forth.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: ASSISTANCE FOR AGRICULTURAL SETTLEMENT AND REHABILITATION AND DEVELOPMENT OF NATURAL AND OTHER RESOURCES
speechtext: A national employment commission, not a council.

subtopic: ASSISTANCE FOR AGRICULTURAL SETTLEMENT AND REHABILITATION AND DEVELOPMENT OF NATURAL AND OTHER RESOURCES
speechtext:
Yes, I stand corrected in that-a national employment commission. When that bill was under discussion I pointed out that there would be difficulty in securing action through that commission because of a section which provided for funds to be voted by parliament, and limiting it to that. I indicated then that it might well be that works that would be proposed could not be proceeded with imtil after the next session of parliament. That position was somewhat questioned by the government, I believe by the Prime Minister himself, as being a bit unreasonable. Now in this Bill No. 19 we have passed subsection 1 of section 3 which empowers the government to authorize the execution of certain works and undertakings which the government may consider to be in the general interest of the country. Then this subsection that we are dealing with provides that in such works unemployed persons may be engaged. All of this is very good provided it can be made effective. But as the hon. member for Vancouver-Burrard (Mr. McGeer) has pointed out, in the subsequent section all these agreements are made subject to approval:
No agreement entered into under the provisions of this section shall be binding upon the dominion until approved by resolution of the House of Commons.
We have this situation: a commission has been set up which cannot possibly get into action for some months, and then, whether it is done by the commission or by the minister, when certain works and things that would be helpful are decided upon, none of these can become effective until approved by parliament. If we are sincerely desirous of making
Unemployment

a contribution, to the relief of unemployment by this process of agreements with the provinces and with corporations, partnerships and individuals, we must make it possible for the commission and the government to act this year, this summer, immediately, or whenever these matters come to a head. Otherwise parliament will be making itself ridiculous, authorizing the making of agreements and then tying the hands of the government. So that while it may 'be more or less _ out of order to refer at this point to subsection 2 of section 4, we must anticipate these matters as we proceed. I think the government should be prepared to amend that subsection, and if they would indicate now an intention to do so it would remove the questions in my mind as to the usefulness of the preceding section of the bill. I suggest to the minister-or to the Prime Minister; it seems to me it is a question of the policy of the government- that if the government desire to attack vigorously this problem, every measure we pass should be founded upon that determination. I think the minister is quite sincere in his desire to cope with this question, and he has my entire sympathy in view of the complex and harassing nature of it; but I am bound to say that for some time past I have recognized that this will tie our hands, and I would remind the minister of my observations in connection with Bill No. 14, which apply as well to this bill.

subtopic: ASSISTANCE FOR AGRICULTURAL SETTLEMENT AND REHABILITATION AND DEVELOPMENT OF NATURAL AND OTHER RESOURCES
speechtext:

definite answers on two points with respect to which I think the minister should give some information. about men who are unemployed. I go back to the situation I mentioned before the recess. There are in my own city 5,000 unemployed men. Out of that number 800 who were eating that day were transients. The

Unemployment
policy of our cities is to shift those men on after two days. That is being done in Ottawa; we feed them a couple of days and then tell them to get out-anywhere, we don't care where, but "get out." Then when they get to the next town they may feed them for a day or two, and then the order is, "get out. ' It seems to me at some point that chain has to be broken. Those men have to be located at some point where there is work.

subtopic: ASSISTANCE FOR AGRICULTURAL SETTLEMENT AND REHABILITATION AND DEVELOPMENT OF NATURAL AND OTHER RESOURCES
speechtext: Has my hon. friend any suggestion in that regard?

subtopic: ASSISTANCE FOR AGRICULTURAL SETTLEMENT AND REHABILITATION AND DEVELOPMENT OF NATURAL AND OTHER RESOURCES
speechtext: Yes; I think there ought to be some definite policy under which, if there is work available, men wmuld be given free transportation from the point they are now being kept on relief to the point where work would be supplied. I suggest there should be a registry, and that in some way this aimless going from place to place be stopped. That is one thing that ought to be included, and I hope the minister will give it serious consideration. Then there is another point concerning which my colleague did not receive a very clear answer from the minister. Is there any guarantee that the men who are going to work on the farms will get as high wages as those being placed in the railway camps?

subtopic: ASSISTANCE FOR AGRICULTURAL SETTLEMENT AND REHABILITATION AND DEVELOPMENT OF NATURAL AND OTHER RESOURCES
speechtext: The answer is perfectly clear: the government has no control over wages being paid by farmers to those who accept employment on farms.

subtopic: ASSISTANCE FOR AGRICULTURAL SETTLEMENT AND REHABILITATION AND DEVELOPMENT OF NATURAL AND OTHER RESOURCES
speechtext: But the government has control over the wages to be paid to the men in the railway camps. Surely if it has control over the wages paid to men on the railways it could have control over those paid to men on the farms. If the farmers cannot pay, then it would seem as reasonable to subsidize the farmer as it is to subsidize the railway companies. If we insist upon a wage in the railway camps for one group of men, and permit others to go to the farms and receive smaller wages-not so much because the farmer will not pay it, but because he cannot-there is bound to be no end of trouble.

subtopic: ASSISTANCE FOR AGRICULTURAL SETTLEMENT AND REHABILITATION AND DEVELOPMENT OF NATURAL AND OTHER RESOURCES
speechtext: It has always been so.

subtopic: ASSISTANCE FOR AGRICULTURAL SETTLEMENT AND REHABILITATION AND DEVELOPMENT OF NATURAL AND OTHER RESOURCES
speechtext: The hon. member must be aware that there is a variety of wage scales in different occupations. I know of no way by which one could assure a complete parity of wage scales maintained in various occupations.

subtopic: ASSISTANCE FOR AGRICULTURAL SETTLEMENT AND REHABILITATION AND DEVELOPMENT OF NATURAL AND OTHER RESOURCES
speechtext: But surely the minister knows that there is a fairly standard wage which is supposed to be paid by the farmer. I believe in the past we have subsidized the farmer to the extent of five dollars; I think that is correct.

subtopic: ASSISTANCE FOR AGRICULTURAL SETTLEMENT AND REHABILITATION AND DEVELOPMENT OF NATURAL AND OTHER RESOURCES
speechtext: In the winter time.

subtopic: ASSISTANCE FOR AGRICULTURAL SETTLEMENT AND REHABILITATION AND DEVELOPMENT OF NATURAL AND OTHER RESOURCES
speechtext: The provinces made a contribution for some time.

subtopic: ASSISTANCE FOR AGRICULTURAL SETTLEMENT AND REHABILITATION AND DEVELOPMENT OF NATURAL AND OTHER RESOURCES
speechtext: That is an arrangement as between the dominion and the provinces. But my point is that if we can subsidize them to the extent of five dollars, and find that that amount is not sufficient, could we not subsidize to the extent of fifteen dollars, or whatever is necessary, so as to bring the wage up to a reasonable standard, or at least to the rate paid in the railway camps? I cannot see any reason why men in the railway camps should be subsidized to a greater extent than men working for farmers. I do not see why there should be a difference between those two sets of wages.

subtopic: ASSISTANCE FOR AGRICULTURAL SETTLEMENT AND REHABILITATION AND DEVELOPMENT OF NATURAL AND OTHER RESOURCES
speechtext: So far as the railway work is concerned, it is not a subsidy at all. I believe it was made clear some time ago that the government is cooperating with the railways in making the work available during the present year, and we adopted that scheme as one means of closing the relief camps, being strongly of the view that relief camps must be closed, and further of the view that if they are closed we must seek to find some alternative employment for the men now in the camps.

subtopic: ASSISTANCE FOR AGRICULTURAL SETTLEMENT AND REHABILITATION AND DEVELOPMENT OF NATURAL AND OTHER RESOURCES
speechtext:
Does the minister
mean to say the government is giving no money to the railways?

subtopic: ASSISTANCE FOR AGRICULTURAL SETTLEMENT AND REHABILITATION AND DEVELOPMENT OF NATURAL AND OTHER RESOURCES
speechtext: No, certainly not.

subtopic: ASSISTANCE FOR AGRICULTURAL SETTLEMENT AND REHABILITATION AND DEVELOPMENT OF NATURAL AND OTHER RESOURCES
speechtext:
The railways are
undertaking the whole cost?

subtopic: ASSISTANCE FOR AGRICULTURAL SETTLEMENT AND REHABILITATION AND DEVELOPMENT OF NATURAL AND OTHER RESOURCES
speechtext: No, there is no suggestion of that at all. I said the government is entering into a cooperative scheme with the railway companies, the full terms of which, as I said earlier to-day, will be placed before the house in due course. But the government is assisting the railways, and the railways are thus entering into a wage relationship with the men who will do the work.

subtopic: ASSISTANCE FOR AGRICULTURAL SETTLEMENT AND REHABILITATION AND DEVELOPMENT OF NATURAL AND OTHER RESOURCES
speechtext: I am not worrying about the exact form of the assistance. The minister admits the government is assisting the railways.

subtopic: ASSISTANCE FOR AGRICULTURAL SETTLEMENT AND REHABILITATION AND DEVELOPMENT OF NATURAL AND OTHER RESOURCES
speechtext:
Yes, certainly.
Unemployment

subtopic: ASSISTANCE FOR AGRICULTURAL SETTLEMENT AND REHABILITATION AND DEVELOPMENT OF NATURAL AND OTHER RESOURCES
speechtext:
And my point is
that if it assists the railways, and if through that assistance the railways are able to employ a number of these men, I cannot see why the government could not assist the farmers and help them at least to equal the wage paid by the railways, or the current wage.

subtopic: ASSISTANCE FOR AGRICULTURAL SETTLEMENT AND REHABILITATION AND DEVELOPMENT OF NATURAL AND OTHER RESOURCES
speechtext: At the time the relief camp policy was announced it was made clear that in the neighbourhood of 20,000 men were in the camps. As I said a minute ago we felt we could not close the camps without affording the men in them an opportunity for alternative employment. One direction in which alternative employment could be secured-and it seemed to us a constructive direction-was in connection with deferred maintenance work on the railway systems of Canada. That would make provision for 10,000 men. We have determined to make every effort to secure alternative employment for the remaining 10,000 up until the camps close. In the meantime we increased allowances in such a way as to give^ these men at least some stake for industrial reestablishment when on July 1 they leave the camps. Those two elements of the policy appeared to be complementary, one to the other. We are now making and shall continue to make every effort to secure alternative employment for the men in the camps.

subtopic: ASSISTANCE FOR AGRICULTURAL SETTLEMENT AND REHABILITATION AND DEVELOPMENT OF NATURAL AND OTHER RESOURCES
speechtext:
I understand that at the
present time the approximate cost of maintaining a man in a camp is about $50. Surely it would be cheaper to subsidize agriculture to the extent of $15 rather than maintain the men in camps at a cost of $50.

subtopic: ASSISTANCE FOR AGRICULTURAL SETTLEMENT AND REHABILITATION AND DEVELOPMENT OF NATURAL AND OTHER RESOURCES
speechtext: Does the minister corroborate the figure of $50, which has been given so frequently?

subtopic: ASSISTANCE FOR AGRICULTURAL SETTLEMENT AND REHABILITATION AND DEVELOPMENT OF NATURAL AND OTHER RESOURCES
speechtext:
No. I was going to say
that our advice, which I believe is accurate, is that the total cost is $1.28 per day.

subtopic: ASSISTANCE FOR AGRICULTURAL SETTLEMENT AND REHABILITATION AND DEVELOPMENT OF NATURAL AND OTHER RESOURCES
speechtext:
Including the new wage
scale?

subtopic: ASSISTANCE FOR AGRICULTURAL SETTLEMENT AND REHABILITATION AND DEVELOPMENT OF NATURAL AND OTHER RESOURCES
speechtext: That was prior to the new wage scale.

subtopic: ASSISTANCE FOR AGRICULTURAL SETTLEMENT AND REHABILITATION AND DEVELOPMENT OF NATURAL AND OTHER RESOURCES
speechtext:
Does that include all
expenses of the camp?

subtopic: ASSISTANCE FOR AGRICULTURAL SETTLEMENT AND REHABILITATION AND DEVELOPMENT OF NATURAL AND OTHER RESOURCES
speechtext: Yes.

subtopic: ASSISTANCE FOR AGRICULTURAL SETTLEMENT AND REHABILITATION AND DEVELOPMENT OF NATURAL AND OTHER RESOURCES
speechtext:
Sessional paper 102B
signed by the Secretary of State and the Minister of Mines, in answer to my question asked during the present session, places the figure at $50.70. A list of 162 camps is given, and there are figures showing the cost per

month per man in each camp. Those figures, signed as I have indicated, are on file. Either they are in error or the statement by the minister is in error. Certainly the two do not jibe.

subtopic: ASSISTANCE FOR AGRICULTURAL SETTLEMENT AND REHABILITATION AND DEVELOPMENT OF NATURAL AND OTHER RESOURCES
speechtext: The average cost of maintaining a man in a camp in Alberta is $42.

subtopic: ASSISTANCE FOR AGRICULTURAL SETTLEMENT AND REHABILITATION AND DEVELOPMENT OF NATURAL AND OTHER RESOURCES
speechtext:
Undoubtedly there is a
variation in the costs as between one district and another.

subtopic: ASSISTANCE FOR AGRICULTURAL SETTLEMENT AND REHABILITATION AND DEVELOPMENT OF NATURAL AND OTHER RESOURCES
speechtext:
That is the point I make.
I am asking the minister if it would not be more economical and more satisfactory to assist agriculture by subsidizing the wage to the extent of $15 rather than to maintain these men at $42.

subtopic: ASSISTANCE FOR AGRICULTURAL SETTLEMENT AND REHABILITATION AND DEVELOPMENT OF NATURAL AND OTHER RESOURCES
speechtext: Yes, certainly; I would not contradict that. That is one reason why we are seeking to close the relief camps as soon as possible. We felt that they did not provide an economical or otherwise satisfactory method of providing relief to single homeless men.

subtopic: ASSISTANCE FOR AGRICULTURAL SETTLEMENT AND REHABILITATION AND DEVELOPMENT OF NATURAL AND OTHER RESOURCES
speechtext: Is there any intention on the part of the government to give that subsidy to the farmers so that they may offer employment?

subtopic: ASSISTANCE FOR AGRICULTURAL SETTLEMENT AND REHABILITATION AND DEVELOPMENT OF NATURAL AND OTHER RESOURCES
speechtext: In the past there has been provision for a farm placement scheme.

subtopic: ASSISTANCE FOR AGRICULTURAL SETTLEMENT AND REHABILITATION AND DEVELOPMENT OF NATURAL AND OTHER RESOURCES
speechtext: In the winter.

subtopic: ASSISTANCE FOR AGRICULTURAL SETTLEMENT AND REHABILITATION AND DEVELOPMENT OF NATURAL AND OTHER RESOURCES
speechtext: And in the future there will be provision for a farm placement scheme. In the past however it has applied only during the winter months. At this time I am not in a position to say whether it will be continued in the summer months. All I can say is we are fully cognizant of the importance of the agricultural situation, as it has been discussed by various members this afternoon, and I can assure the committee that the observations made will receive careful consideration. In the past the farm placement scheme has applied only in the winter months when it was particularly desirable to secure food and shelter for single homeless men. To my knowledge there has been no extension of the scheme to that period of the year when under normal circumstances the farmers employ help for seeding and harvesting operations.

subtopic: ASSISTANCE FOR AGRICULTURAL SETTLEMENT AND REHABILITATION AND DEVELOPMENT OF NATURAL AND OTHER RESOURCES
speechtext:
There is one point that has been worrying me ever since the government brought down its program concerning unemployment. Presumably we are making plans to provide work for these unemployed single men until parliament meets again next year. In the past the single homeless unemployed

Unemployment
have been provided for in these camps; otherwise they would have been absolutely without food and shelter unless they were looked after by the municipalities. Now what is worrying me is this: When fall and the cold weather comes and we have just as many unemployed as we have right now, as it is possible we will, what does the government intend to do with those who were looked after last year and the year before in these camps? The largest single unemployed camp in Canada is in Rosthern constituency, at Dundurn, and I know young people who have been very glad to get food and shelter there year after year. Perhaps they have not been entirely sat.sfied but at all events the camp has looked after them. Now we are going to close these camps, and they are to stay closed. What will be done to look after these people next winter?

subtopic: ASSISTANCE FOR AGRICULTURAL SETTLEMENT AND REHABILITATION AND DEVELOPMENT OF NATURAL AND OTHER RESOURCES
speechtext: The provision made for at least a large number of those in the relief camps through their employment on deferred maintenance work on the railways ought to . enable them to provide for themselves during the coming winter, particularly if they are able to defer the expenditure of a portion of that money until the winter months. I am assuming that they have five or six months' employment on the railways. They are single men, and I say that ought to suffice to carry them through the winter months, certainly in a far more satisfactory way than they could have provided for themselves under any alternative form of relief employment.

subtopic: ASSISTANCE FOR AGRICULTURAL SETTLEMENT AND REHABILITATION AND DEVELOPMENT OF NATURAL AND OTHER RESOURCES
speechtext: Is there any provision being made to hold back part of their pay so that they will have something for the winter months?

subtopic: ASSISTANCE FOR AGRICULTURAL SETTLEMENT AND REHABILITATION AND DEVELOPMENT OF NATURAL AND OTHER RESOURCES
speechtext: There is provision for deferred pay so far as camp workers are concerned. It is probably beyond our competence to ensure that there'shall be deferred pay so far as the railway work is concerned.

subtopic: ASSISTANCE FOR AGRICULTURAL SETTLEMENT AND REHABILITATION AND DEVELOPMENT OF NATURAL AND OTHER RESOURCES
speechtext: Could the minister give us any idea how much a month these boys will be able to make on the railways?

subtopic: ASSISTANCE FOR AGRICULTURAL SETTLEMENT AND REHABILITATION AND DEVELOPMENT OF NATURAL AND OTHER RESOURCES
speechtext: I am really not in a position to give that information in advance of the submission to the house of the agreement. All I can assure my hon. friend is this, that they will receive the prevailing wages for extra gang work done by the railways.

subtopic: ASSISTANCE FOR AGRICULTURAL SETTLEMENT AND REHABILITATION AND DEVELOPMENT OF NATURAL AND OTHER RESOURCES
speechtext: Did the minister mention twenty-five cents an hour?

subtopic: ASSISTANCE FOR AGRICULTURAL SETTLEMENT AND REHABILITATION AND DEVELOPMENT OF NATURAL AND OTHER RESOURCES
speechtext: No, I did not make that statement.

subtopic: ASSISTANCE FOR AGRICULTURAL SETTLEMENT AND REHABILITATION AND DEVELOPMENT OF NATURAL AND OTHER RESOURCES
speechtext: But the policy of the government next fall will be determined by the rate of wages that prevails, and if we do not know what the rate of wages is to be we cannot properly decide upon a policy. If it is just going to be a subsistence allowance, there is no use in calling it wages. It may amount to only about twenty cents a day, which is what they were getting in the camps.

subtopic: ASSISTANCE FOR AGRICULTURAL SETTLEMENT AND REHABILITATION AND DEVELOPMENT OF NATURAL AND OTHER RESOURCES
speechtext:
There is another
grievous matter which we must look into with great care. When these boys go out on the railway maintenance work, is their clothing to be provided for them, or have they to buy it out of what they earn? What about their board and other matters of that kind? If they are not going to receive enough per month on their railway job to provide them with the necessities of life and allow them to save up enough to go through next winter, provide themselves with a room in town and their board and all that sort of thing, we cannot blame any intelligent young man for being filled with grave anxiety at the prospect of going out. I know from personal experience that many times the boys are taken in by propositions of this kind. They will go out with a construction gang, and then they will find that more than half their income is eaten up by their board and clothing and the like. They then are docked for the days they are unable to work, and when they get through with the job they find that they are simply out. If there is no guarantee whatsoever that when this railway work is over they are going back to relief camps, or no guarantee to ensure them of some sort of security during the winter months, they will face the future with grave apprehension.
So far as farm work is concerned, the information thus far elicited gives no guarantee for their future at all. If they are going to get $15 a month on the farm and have their employment cut off about the middle of October when farm work finishes, and have no idea of what they are going to do or where they are going to go for the winter, I cannot blame these young men for being filled with alarm. It is easy enough for us to talk about these things here, but when we see the actual situation the boys will face, it is really heartbreaking.
There is another question I would ask in connection with transients. I have come in contact with cases which have brought this matter vividly to my attention. Is there any provision now whereby a transient can go into some office and register himself as a seeker after employment? The condition as brought to our attention by the hon. member for Broadview (Mr. Church) is most deplorable.

Unemployment
If when boys without any money are out on the road or in the city seeking work as earnestly as anyone could, they then can be taken up and punished; that is a criminal thing for any government to tolerate. It is simply dreadful. It fills the boys with bitterness. I have seen boys in the last few weeks in that condition. Unless some arrangement is made to protect them it is simply terrible. Has the government a registration bureau, for example, at which the young man can report when he is seeking employment? I should like to contribute this little bit, Mr. Chairman, in kindness to and sympathy for the minister. I should like to know whether these matters have been looked into in detail, so that next fall and winter the boys will not be stranded and suffering from one end of this country to the other.

subtopic: ASSISTANCE FOR AGRICULTURAL SETTLEMENT AND REHABILITATION AND DEVELOPMENT OF NATURAL AND OTHER RESOURCES
speechtext:
So far as transients are
concerned, perhaps my hon. friend is aware that in most of the large towns and cities there is an employment office at which transients can register for employment at any time they desire. I am not aware of any criminal proceedings taken against transients, of which the hon. gentleman has spoken. I could only explain it upon the ground of some other charge than the mere fact that they were going from place to place to seek work. Certainly no prosecutions have been carried forward under any policy sanctioned by this or any other government of Canada. It is conceivable that some transients may fall within the general designation of vagrants.

subtopic: ASSISTANCE FOR AGRICULTURAL SETTLEMENT AND REHABILITATION AND DEVELOPMENT OF NATURAL AND OTHER RESOURCES
speechtext:
They are being
picked un right along for vagrancy, trespassing, and so on.

subtopic: ASSISTANCE FOR AGRICULTURAL SETTLEMENT AND REHABILITATION AND DEVELOPMENT OF NATURAL AND OTHER RESOURCES
speechtext: Where?

subtopic: ASSISTANCE FOR AGRICULTURAL SETTLEMENT AND REHABILITATION AND DEVELOPMENT OF NATURAL AND OTHER RESOURCES
speechtext: All over the country.

subtopic: ASSISTANCE FOR AGRICULTURAL SETTLEMENT AND REHABILITATION AND DEVELOPMENT OF NATURAL AND OTHER RESOURCES
speechtext:
I am still not satisfied,
Mr. Chairman. The suggestion is made that ten thousand men will get work on the railways. There was more than twice that number, speaking from memory, in the unemployment camps last winter. We are going to put ten thousand to work on the railways. We do not know how much they will receive, or how much they will be able to save. It is very likely that, not having had any money for some time, they will spend a little bit more than absolutely necessary, like everybody else. But suppose they do save a little; what about the other ten thousand who are not given this work? Suppose, further, some of those who are given the work spend what they earn; what is going to happen to them next winter? That is what is worrying me. The unemployment camps are not an ideal way of 
looking after these men, but they were good enough to induce single unemployed men to go to them and get food and shelter from the cold weather we have in this country. I want to know what the government intends to do to take the place of these camps next winter, to look after people who have no money to look after themselves. Has the government any plans for looking after these men? H the government has none at the present time, will the government agree that if the camps are not reopened these men will be looked after in some way, perhaps by making grants to farmers to provide for them? Will the government give consideration to this problem? I am satisfied that, as surely as I am standing here, there will be a problem this coming winter if no provision is made for looking after these people. If no provision is made for them and they are thrown on the cities and the cities cannot look after them we shall have riots; there will be a good deal of trouble. If the government has no plans, does it intend to work out plans to look after these men? I have had some experience with young people and I know what it will mean for these 10.000 men who are going to be employed on the railways. How long will they be able to keep themselves in the winter out of what they have been able to save from what they make on the railways? It seems to me that we should have some assurance that when the camps are closed something will be done to take their place next year if necessary.

subtopic: ASSISTANCE FOR AGRICULTURAL SETTLEMENT AND REHABILITATION AND DEVELOPMENT OF NATURAL AND OTHER RESOURCES
speechtext:
I have already explained that in the past the government has made good use of farm placement schemes for single homeless men during the winter months, and I have already made the statement that we have it in mind to extend the facilities for farm placement during the coming year. My hon. friend has misgivings as to what will happen to these 10,000 men who will accept employment on the railways during the summer months. I may say that I share his concern for these men though I do not at the moment share his misgivings as to their position during the coming winter. It would be utterly beyond the power of this government to guarantee the employment of these men any more than it can guarantee the employment of any section of the population. We cannot do that; it would be wholly unreasonable for my hon. friend to expect that. I can assure him, however, that during the summer months we shall have the situation under review and if next winter a condition arises that necessitates further care being given to those men who are deserving of it they will receive it.

Unemployment

subtopic: ASSISTANCE FOR AGRICULTURAL SETTLEMENT AND REHABILITATION AND DEVELOPMENT OF NATURAL AND OTHER RESOURCES
speechtext:
While it may be beyond the power of this government to provide employment, it is not beyond the power of the government to take care of the men. The average wage on the railways will be thirty-five cents an hour, and on -the assumption that the men are employed for six months they will get $400, out of which they must provide for everything, and in addition must keep themselves during the other six months of the year. That is what we are up against.
I am not very much concerned whether the government finds employment for the people next winter. If the minister has in mind such schemes as we have had in the past, for instance, giving farm help $5 a month, then I believe this is a reflection on the intelligence of the government. Such a scheme has been tried and found wanting, and it is something which should be resisted by every red-blooded Canadian, because after all it is getting back to feudalism. It is not progress; it is going backwards when you give a man a pittance of $5 a month to work on a farm. So long as the government concentrates its attention on employment, very little will be done; it should concentrate its attention on providing a living for the people of Canada.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: ASSISTANCE FOR AGRICULTURAL SETTLEMENT AND REHABILITATION AND DEVELOPMENT OF NATURAL AND OTHER RESOURCES
speechtext: Does my hon. friend suggest that the government should not seek to find measures for providing employment for the unemployed?

subtopic: ASSISTANCE FOR AGRICULTURAL SETTLEMENT AND REHABILITATION AND DEVELOPMENT OF NATURAL AND OTHER RESOURCES
speechtext: I do not think that is the problem which confronts us. Employment itself is not virtuous; employment is only a means to production; that is all. We have the goods and that is why people are not employed. What we need to do is to monetize the goods, and to do so without putting Canada into debt we must utilize the national credit.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: ASSISTANCE FOR AGRICULTURAL SETTLEMENT AND REHABILITATION AND DEVELOPMENT OF NATURAL AND OTHER RESOURCES
speechtext: The government's policy is to endeavour to find employment for men who are unemployed. If my hon. friend's view is that such is not the right policy I regret that we have to differ with him as to what is wisest. Certainly, however, with respect to the question of unemployment in Canada today, the government is of the view that its first duty, the first obligation of the state, is to endeavour to assist those who are unemployed to find profitable employment.

subtopic: ASSISTANCE FOR AGRICULTURAL SETTLEMENT AND REHABILITATION AND DEVELOPMENT OF NATURAL AND OTHER RESOURCES
speechtext: What would be the purpose of employment? Would it be because employment is a necessity or would it be to provide wages?

subtopic: ASSISTANCE FOR AGRICULTURAL SETTLEMENT AND REHABILITATION AND DEVELOPMENT OF NATURAL AND OTHER RESOURCES
speechtext: Oh, oh.

subtopic: ASSISTANCE FOR AGRICULTURAL SETTLEMENT AND REHABILITATION AND DEVELOPMENT OF NATURAL AND OTHER RESOURCES
speechtext: That is all right, but I do not think the hon. gentleman who interrupts has scratched below the economic surface. Some believe that people live to work; we do not.

subtopic: ASSISTANCE FOR AGRICULTURAL SETTLEMENT AND REHABILITATION AND DEVELOPMENT OF NATURAL AND OTHER RESOURCES
speechtext: Oh, oh.

subtopic: ASSISTANCE FOR AGRICULTURAL SETTLEMENT AND REHABILITATION AND DEVELOPMENT OF NATURAL AND OTHER RESOURCES
speechtext:
The only purpose of work is to produce, and in this country we have the goods but we have not the purchasing power.
I understand the difficulties that the government faces in this transitional period, but I would ask the Prime Minister this question: He speaks of providing employment, and I am trying to get his point of view. Is it because employment in itself is virtuous? Is it because it is absolutely necessary?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: ASSISTANCE FOR AGRICULTURAL SETTLEMENT AND REHABILITATION AND DEVELOPMENT OF NATURAL AND OTHER RESOURCES
speechtext:
The policy of the government is to endeavour to help men to obtain employment in order that they may earn an honest living. If any man is not prepared to work with that object in view the state should not recognize any further obligation towards him. But so long as a man is willing and ready to work it is at times such as the present clearly a duty of the state to help him to find means of getting profitable employment which will enable him to make an honest living for himself and to provide for others who may be dependent upon him.
Mr. PO'OLE: Provided he was willing and ready to work and work was not there, what would the government do then?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: ASSISTANCE FOR AGRICULTURAL SETTLEMENT AND REHABILITATION AND DEVELOPMENT OF NATURAL AND OTHER RESOURCES
speechtext: I have answered that question; I have pointed out that such is the position many are now in. In the country there are, unfortunately, thousands of men who are out of work and who are ready and willing to work if they can find employment. While they are unable to get work the state up to the present has been supplying relief, but every man in whom there is true manhood will prefer work to relief. What the government of the day is seeking to do is, therefore, to provide means whereby those who are unemployed will be enabled to find work.

subtopic: ASSISTANCE FOR AGRICULTURAL SETTLEMENT AND REHABILITATION AND DEVELOPMENT OF NATURAL AND OTHER RESOURCES
speechtext: May I ask another question. I know it is quite a long story but I would ask the Prime Minister this question: Why is it that people cannot find work now? Is it not because we can produce without those who are now unemployed? Is that not true?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: ASSISTANCE FOR AGRICULTURAL SETTLEMENT AND REHABILITATION AND DEVELOPMENT OF NATURAL AND OTHER RESOURCES
speechtext:
I do not think anyone can produce without working and I do not think anyone can hope to live at the expense of the state without working. It is
Unemployment

a deplorable condition of mind if anyone ever comes to the point where he hopes he will get through life without working. Work is not dishonourable; it is the absence of the desire to work that is dishonourable.

subtopic: ASSISTANCE FOR AGRICULTURAL SETTLEMENT AND REHABILITATION AND DEVELOPMENT OF NATURAL AND OTHER RESOURCES
speechtext: Why are so many people unemployed?

subtopic: ASSISTANCE FOR AGRICULTURAL SETTLEMENT AND REHABILITATION AND DEVELOPMENT OF NATURAL AND OTHER RESOURCES
speechtext: The hon. gentleman made an erroneous statement in regard to the unemployed. It is not true that the men get only twenty cents a day. That is a glib statement which is made throughout the country, and it is false. They get more than twenty cents a day; they get their food and clothing. I would not make any statement as false as that.

subtopic: ASSISTANCE FOR AGRICULTURAL SETTLEMENT AND REHABILITATION AND DEVELOPMENT OF NATURAL AND OTHER RESOURCES
speechtext:
I should like to get an answer to the question I asked. Earlier in the debate I made the statement that the average cost per man per month in total for the camps was $50.70, and the minister called that figure in question and gave another. There is a discrepancy between the figures and I should like to have it cleared up, because after all the only thing we can go by is the information we received in sessional papers. I have before me sessional paper No. 102B giving answers to certain questions I asked on February 26. The minister stated that in order to look after this problem as it should be looked after it might be necessary to give some consideration to the extension of the farm placement scheme. I am in entire accord with this policy, as I agree with the hon. member for Portage la Prairie (Mr. Leader) when he states that if it is going to cost around $50 per month to look after these people in camps, they could be looked after for less much better and more satisfactorily in the farm homes of this country where they would not be segregated by themselves as they are in camps. This would be a much better policy in every way than placing these men in camps. I assume that such a

Unemployment
scheme would be the result of agreements between the dominion and the provinces and as I understand it, under subsection 2 of section 4, no such agreement would be valid until it had been approved by resolution of this House of Commons. I should like to know whether the government intends to make agreements with the provinces to take care of this problem which will probably become acute before parliament meets again. Will the government take care of this matter by making the necessary agreements with all the provinces and having those agreements approved by parliament before we prorogue? subtopic: ASSISTANCE FOR AGRICULTURAL SETTLEMENT AND REHABILITATION AND DEVELOPMENT OF NATURAL AND OTHER RESOURCES
speechtext:
On behalf of the city of Vancouver I took this matter up with the provincial government in Victoria, and I was informed that they could do nothing with reference to their association with municipal problems until such time as they could find out what could be done with the dominion government. They were not prepared to entertain any proposal for cooperation between the provincial government and any municipality until they knew the policy of the dominion government. This means that at the moment we cannot deal with the provincial governments.
We are told that the camps are to be closed, and I am afraid that there can be very little real merit in the minister's suggestion that a few months' work on the railways will provide the unemployed who were in the camps with a sustenance allowance for the winter months. Even though a man had worked in the past, after working at these wages and being thrown out of employment he will find himself destitute. These men will crowd into the cities if there are no camps to go to. At the present time
we have something more than the mere unemployed and destitute to deal with; we have to deal with public opinion. On my return to Vancouver I was surprised1 to learn that the police in that city were trying to enforce the bylaws which prevented the holding of tag-days and that sort of thing. They arrested certain men and brought them before a magistrate. The magistrate said that these men were entitled to earn a living; that as far as he was concerned, sitting as a magistrate, he was not going to be a party to persecuting them and that he would not punish them. Public opinion was overwhelmingly in favour of that sentiment.
The problem of the municipalities is not merely that of taking care of the unemployed; it concerns the protecting of the life and property of the individual. Law enforcement falls upon the municipal administrators. If you are going to close these camps and not provide an adequate program of employment, there will develop in the cities, particularly in British Columbia in which there is during the winter months a heavy concentration of unemployed from all over the west, a situation which will prove to be of grave and serious concern for the peace, order and good government of these cities and the liberty and security of every individual in them. It was because of this that I asked the government what agreements they had in mind other than those with the railways. I assumed that under the latter part of subsection 1, of section 4, which provides for agreements with corporations, partnerships or individuals engaged in industry respecting the expansion of industrial employment, provision would be made for some program of employment being developed. However, I take it from the minister's answer that no such program is in contemplation; that the only agreements being considered are the general ones with the provinces providing for some contributory form of assistance. It may be laudable and advisable to close these relief camps, but I contend it is a desperate and dangerous thing to do if no adequate program of employment is developed in the meantime to carry these men through, not only the summer months but the winter months as well.

I think I have assured the committee already that we shall take every possible means of ensuring that the employment of these men will continue as long as possible. It was announced that the allowances in the relief camps would be increased to $15 per month

on February 29. A reasonable inference from that surely would be that these men were going to their own homes; that they were going to some other employment which gave them a greater wage than $15 a month with board and lodging, or that they did not wish to remain in the camps and work as they were obliged to do under the new policy.

As a matter of fact I
think anyone who is conversant with the relief camp situation knows exactly what happens every year. There is a large number of men, just about the number mentioned by the minister, who, as soon as spring comes and weather conditions make it possible, leave the camps. Most of them leave not to go to work but to roam about as adventurers and to "hit the road."
